newsitem.title: USA: BP demonstrates new acrylonitrile process.
newsitem.headline: BP demonstrates new acrylonitrile process.

text.p: BP Chemicals Inc said Thursday it has successfully operated a first-stage demonstration unit for the production of acrylonitrile from propane ammoxidation.
Acrylonitrile is a key building block for acrylic fibers, plastics and nitrile rubber, the British Petroleum Co Plc subsidiary said.

BP Chemicals said the propane process offers 20 percent lower production costs compared to the current propylene route, and also the potential for significant additional cost reductions, as has been the case with BP's propylene process.

The company noted it announced the new propane process in September 1996. Since then BP has been advancing this technology with the aim of basing its acrylonitrile capacity investments in the next decade on propane as a feedstock.

"The completion, startup and sustained operation of this unit is a key milestone in the confirmation of our expectations for this process' commercialization," said Richard Smith, senior vice president, Technology and Business Development, BP Chemicals. "We are very pleased that the catalyst and process are meeting our expectations."
He said BP is "considering process implementation options which may be applicable to existing plant conversions, as well as new builds."
BP Chemicals' interest in propane ammoxidation began several years ago when the company decided to explore a one-step catalytic process for producing acrylonitrile from propane, ammonia and oxygen.
The company does not discuss the catalyst used in the process, spokesman Tony Kozlowski said.

Contributing to propane's economic advantages are increased production of valuable co-products, lower by-product waste formation, and, in various parts of the world, a cost and availability advantage over propylene, BP said.
On an overall cost basis, the propane process is advantaged over facilities which generate their propylene feedstock via propane dehydrogenation, BP said.
